Me Generation
MEE jen-er-AY-shun
noun (Boomer slang)
From Tom Wolfe’s essay "The ‘Me’ Decade and the Third Great Awakening," New York magazine, August 23, 1976, which described the 1970s turn from 1960s politics to self-exploration: est seminars, encounter groups, jogging, therapy, and every kind of personal-growth movement. Me Decade quickly became Me Generation, a label for the Boomers themselves. Christopher Lasch’s The Culture of Narcissism (1979) gave the critique its scholarly form.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Me Generation is the label pinned on the Boomers in the 1970s, when the idealism of the 1960s turned inward: find yourself, actualize yourself, love yourself, look out for number one. Tom Wolfe noticed that the movement was religious in shape — a "Third Great Awakening" with the self at the altar. The Christian observation: Wolfe was right about the religion, and Scripture had named it. "This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud" (2Ti 3:1–2). Lovers of their own selves heads the list; the other sins follow from it. The gospel runs exactly the other way. "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me" (Luk 9:23). "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others" (Php 2:3–4). And the motive is Christ Himself: "For even Christ pleased not himself" (Rom 15:3). The Me Generation sought to find the self and lost it; the gospel promises that the one who loses his life for Christ’s sake will find it. Paul’s testimony is the anti-Me creed: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20). Every generation since has been a Me Generation; the cross is the only cure.

Webster 1828 Definition

Label for the Boomers’ 1970s turn to self-fulfillment (from Tom Wolfe’s "Me Decade," 1976) — the "lovers of their own selves" of 2Ti 3:2, answered by the call to deny self and follow Christ (Luk 9:23).

ME GENERATION, n. (1970s; Boomer era) The generation (chiefly Baby Boomers) characterized in the 1970s by a preoccupation with self-fulfillment, self-expression, and personal gratification. From Me Decade (Tom Wolfe, New York, August 23, 1976).

Webster (1828) — GENERATION, noun The act of begetting; procreation, as of animals. 1. Production; formation; as the generation of sounds or of curves or equations. 2. A single succession in natural descent, as the children of the same parents; hence, an age. Thus we say, the third, the fourth, or the tenth generation Genesis 15:16 . 3. The people of the same period, or living at the same time. O faithless and perverse generation Luke 9:41 . 4. Genealogy; a series of children or descendants from the same stock. This is the book of the generations of Adam. Genesis 5:1 .

Decode for families: every later generation has been called the new Me Generation. The diagnosis is 2Ti 3:2; it fits all of us.

2Ti 3:2 — "For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,"

Luk 9:23 — "And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me."

Php 2:3 — "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves."

Gal 2:20 — "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me."

Modern Corruption

The Me Generation enthroned the self as the object of devotion; Scripture lists self-love first among the sins of the last days and calls the disciple to deny himself.

expand to see more

The 1970s did not invent selfishness, but they gave it a vocabulary of virtue. "Finding yourself," "self-actualization," "self-esteem," and "doing what’s right for me" turned the oldest sin into a program of personal growth. Marriages ended because a spouse needed to grow; children were left because a parent needed space. The therapeutic culture that followed has never looked back. Wolfe’s insight was that this was a religion; Paul’s was that it was idolatry with the self in the idol’s place.

The Christian answer is not self-hatred but self-forgetfulness. Php 2:3–4 does not tell the believer to despise himself but to look also on the things of others. The self is not destroyed in Christ; it is crucified and raised (Gal 2:20). The man who stops asking "What about me?" finds, to his surprise, that God has already answered the question at the cross.
